'''''Cabomba caroliniana''''', commonly known as '''Carolina fanwort''', is a [[rhizomatous]], aquatic, [[perennial]] herb native to North and South America. Having been a popular [[aquarium]] plant, it has been exported around the world and has become an [[invasive species]] in Europe and Australia.

===Cytology===
The [[chromosome]] count is 2n = 26, 78, 104.<ref name = "Flora of China" /> The [[chloroplast]] genome is 164057 bp or 160177 bp long.<ref name = "Gruenstaeudl et al., 2018">Gruenstaeudl, M., Gerschler, N., & Borsch, T. (2018). [https://www.researchgate.net/publication/325925567_Bioinformatic_Workflows_for_Generating_Complete_Plastid_Genome_Sequences-An_Example_from_Cabomba_Cabombaceae_in_the_Context_of_the_Phylogenomic_Analysis_of_the_Water-Lily_Clade Bioinformatic workflows for generating complete plastid genome sequences—an example from ''Cabomba'' (Cabombaceae) in the context of the phylogenomic analysis of the water-lily clade.] Life, 8(3), 25.</ref>

===Similar species===
''[[Limnophila sessiliflora]]'' is similar but has whirls of three or more leaves instead of opposite pairs.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Audubon |url=https://www.google.com/books/edition/National_Audubon_Society_Wildflowers_of/AG-TEAAAQBAJ?hl=en |title=Wildflowers of North America |date=2023 |publisher=Knopf |isbn=978-0-593-31994-9 |location=New York |pages=22}}</ref>

==Common names==
''Cabomba caroliniana'' is commonly called Carolina fanwort,<ref name=PLANTS>{{PLANTS|id=CACA|taxon=Cabomba caroliniana|access-date=10 January 2016}}</ref> Carolina water shield,<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17}}</ref> green cabomba, fanwort, fish grass, Washington grass, Washington plant, common cabomba, Washington plant, and watershield.<ref name=bcc>{{cite web | title=Cabomba | website= Brisbane City Council - Weed Identification Tool| date=31 December 2021 | url=https://weeds.brisbane.qld.gov.au/weeds/cabomba | access-date=13 July 2023}}</ref>

==Ecology==
Large numbers of plants are sent from [[Florida]] to the rest of the U.S. for commercial use. Fanwort is also grown commercially in Asia for export to Europe and other parts of the world. Small-scale, local cultivation occurs in some areas, and [[aquarists]] are probably responsible for some introductions.{{cn|date=July 2023}} 

This species grows rooted in the mud of stagnant to slow-flowing water, including streams, smaller rivers, lakes, ponds, sloughs, and ditches. In some states in the U.S., it is now regarded as a weed. Fanwort stems become brittle in late summer, which causes the plant to break apart, facilitating its distribution and invasion of new water bodies. It produces by seed, but vegetative reproduction seems to be its main vehicle for spreading to new waters. Growth of {{convert|50|mm|abbr=on|frac=2}} a day has been reported in [[Lake Macdonald, Queensland|Lake Macdonald]] in [[Queensland]], Australia.<ref name=grin>{{cite web | title=''Cabomba caroliniana'' | website=[[Global Invasive Species Database]]|date= 4 March 2006| url=http://www.iucngisd.org/gisd/speciesname/Cabomba+caroliniana | access-date=13 July 2023| quote=Principal source: Washington State Department of Ecology, 2003. Technical Information About ''Cabomba caroliniana'' (Fanwort), ERDC, UNDATED ''Cabomba caroliniana'' Gray (Fanwort); Compiler: National Biological Information Infrastructure (NBII) & IUCN/SSC Invasive Species Specialist Group (ISSG)}}</ref>

Use in the [[aquarium]] trade<ref name="Flora of North America" /> has led to some species being [[Introduced species|introduced]] to other parts of the world, such as Australia, where ''Cabomba caroliniana'' it is a nationally declared [[Pest (organism)|weed]].<ref name="EUinv" /><ref name = "NSW WeedWise">{{cite web | title=''Cabomba'' (''Cabomba caroliniana'') | website=NSW WeedWise | date=24 January 2020 | url=https://weeds.dpi.nsw.gov.au/Weeds/Details/26 | access-date=13 July 2023}}</ref> Having arrived in 1967, it spread rapidly in waterways and out-competed native plants, threatening water supplies, especially along the eastern side of the continent.<ref name=nichols2023>{{cite web | last=Nichols | first=Jennifer | title=''Cabomba'' weevil unleashed on weed-infesting Australian waterways | website=[[ABC News (Australia)]] | date=10 July 2023 | url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/rural/2023-07-10/cabomba-weevil-unleashed-on-weed-infesting-australian-waterways/102482954 | access-date=12 July 2023}}</ref> It is a [[Weeds of National Significance|weed of national significance]] in Australia.<ref name="AUinv">{{cite web |url=http://www.weeds.org.au/natsig.htm |title=Weeds Australia - Weeds of National Significance |access-date=2008-10-04 |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20081017220642/http://www.weeds.org.au/natsig.htm |archive-date=2008-10-17 }}</ref>

It is also on the [[List of invasive alien species of Union concern|list of invasive alien species of concern]] in the [[European Union]].<ref name="EUinv">{{cite web|url=http://ec.europa.eu/environment/nature/invasivealien/docs/IAS_list_regulation_annex.pdf |title=Annex to the commission implementing regulation (EU)... adopting a list of invasive alien species of Union concern pursuant to Regulation (EU); No 1143/2014 of the European Parliament and of the Council: List of invasive alien species of Union concern |access-date=2016-07-14 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20160713155109/http://ec.europa.eu/environment/nature/invasivealien/docs/IAS_list_regulation_annex.pdf |archive-date=2016-07-13 }}</ref> The latter implies that the species cannot be traded nor commercialised. The EU forbids trading and selling of the plant and requires people possessing it before the regulation went into force to take appropriate measures to prevent it from spreading.<ref>{{Cite web|date=June 2021|title=European Regulation IAS|url=https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex%3A32014R1143|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150910043414/http://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32014R1143 |archive-date=2015-09-10 }}</ref>
===Control measures===
{{as of|July 2023}} a trial is under way to control the weed by introducing a tiny South American beetle, ''[[Hydrotimetes natans]]'', or ''Cabomba'' weevil, into [[Six Mile Creek Dam|Lake Macdonald]] and [[Lake Kurwongbah]] in Queensland. The species is being bred in a nursery at Kurwongbah, with a view to national introduction for [[biological control]] of the weed. The larvae of the weevil damage the plant by tunnelling through its stems, breaking them down and causing fungal infections which hinder their ability to reproduce. It has been found that only the insect mostly feeds on ''Cabomba'', and does not affect any native plants.<ref name=nichols2023/>

==Conservation==
The [[NatureServe conservation status]] is G5 Secure.<ref name = "NatureServe" />
